paragraphs.heading: The middle of the Milky Way
paragraphs.text: At the heart of the Milky Way lies the Galactic Center, the galaxy's barycenter, which sits on the axis around which the galaxy rotates. Its central massive object is Sagittarius A*, a supermassive black hole with roughly 4 million times the mass of the Sun. From Earth, the center lies roughly 26,000 light-years away, in the direction of Sagittarius, Ophiuchus and Scorpius, the part of the sky where the Milky Way looks brightest.

paragraphs.heading: A crowded core
paragraphs.text: The region is packed with stars: around 10 million of them lie within one parsec of the center. Most are red giants, but there are also many massive supergiants and Wolf–Rayet stars, which came from star formation there about a million years ago. These core stars are only a small piece of a much wider central region called the galactic bulge.

paragraphs.heading: Looking through the dust
paragraphs.text: Dust between us and the center hides it at visible, ultraviolet and soft, low-energy X-ray wavelengths. What we know comes from gamma rays, hard X-rays, infrared, submillimetre and radio. In 1918 Harlow Shapley saw that the halo of globular clusters seemed centered on star swarms in Sagittarius, but dark clouds blocked the view. In the early 1940s Walter Baade used wartime blackouts in Los Angeles to search with the 100-inch Hooker Telescope at Mount Wilson. Near the star Alnasl he found a gap in the dust lanes one degree wide, giving a fairly clear look at the stars around the nucleus, and it has been called Baade's Window ever since.

paragraphs.heading: Found by radio
paragraphs.text: A team of radio astronomers in Sydney, Australia, led by Joseph Lade Pawsey, had built an 80-foot dish by 1954 and used it to study a very powerful belt of radio emission in Sagittarius. They named a strong point source near the middle of the belt Sagittarius A. They realised it lay at the true center of the Galaxy, about 32 degrees south-west of where the center had been assumed to be. In 1958 the International Astronomical Union adopted Sagittarius A as the zero point for galactic latitude and longitude.

paragraphs.heading: The black hole at the heart
paragraphs.text: Within Sagittarius A lies an intense, compact radio source, Sagittarius A*, which matches the position of the supermassive black hole. Gas falling onto the black hole, probably through a disk around it, would release the energy that powers this radio source. In 2008, linked radio telescopes in Hawaii, Arizona and California measured the source at 44 million kilometres across, a little less than the distance from Mercury to the Sun. Scientists at the Max Planck Institute for Extraterrestrial Physics, using telescopes in Chile, confirmed the black hole at roughly 4.3 million solar masses.

paragraphs.heading: Giant bubbles
paragraphs.text: In November 2010 astronomers announced two huge lobes of energetic plasma, called bubbles, on either side of the galaxy's core, glowing in gamma rays and X-rays. Known as the Fermi or eRosita bubbles, they reach about 25,000 light-years above and below the center. Columns of plasma called chimneys connect them to the core. By 2022, detailed computer models backed the view that Sagittarius A* produced them.
